title: Best Practices for Sales Agentic Demos
summary: We sat down with Alex Farman, AI strategy consultant at HiBob to unpack what agentic demos are, when to use them (and when not to), what kind of ROI to expect, and where the future of demos – and SaaS sales in general – is going.
body_markdown:
Giving prospects a way to “try before they buy” has been the goal for GTM SaaS teams for the past decade.


It started with adding product screenshots to the website, then video walkthroughs, and in the past few years,[demo automation](https://www.navattic.com/blog/demo-automation) has become a core part of the toolkit, letting sales and SE teams capture the product once and turn it into an interactive product demo (so prospects can explore key features before or after a live sales call) or a sandbox demo environment.


Now, companies are taking things a step further, asking where and how to embed AI agents into the demo experience.


To get a clear picture of how that’s playing out, we talked to the customers running[agentic demos](https://www.navattic.com/blog/what-are-agentic-demos) in production.


Below, we unpack what agentic demos are, when to use them (and when not to), what kind of ROI to expect, and where the future of demos – and SaaS sales in general – is going.


What Are Agentic Demos?


Like interactive demos,[agentic demos](http://navattic.com/blog/agentic-vs-interactive-demos) educate prospects on the key value props of your product.


But instead of a more traditional, structured click-through, buyers can ask agents to show any part of your product or ask the agent questions about what your product can or cannot do. Think of them as[AI copilot product experts](https://www.navattic.com/blog/agent-demos-announcement) . They can:


- Speak with prospects
- Navigate your product (clicking, typing, scrolling)
- Respond to questions based on defined product context, FAQs, guidelines, and guardrails


As[Alex Farman](https://www.linkedin.com/in/alex-farman-53575a106/) , former AI strategy consultant at[HiBob](https://www.hibob.com/) , puts it:


*“An agentic demo is an interactive demo experience which is trained on the product being demoed and can be as versatile as a ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini. Buyers can have a conversational experience as if they were speaking to a rep and sales engineer.”*


That has three key benefits:


1. **Greater trust.** Buyers can test edge cases and see the product respond in real time, giving them more confidence that your product does what you say it does.
2. **Deeper self-serve education.** Buyers get the information they need without having to speak with sales. Not only is that the way they prefer to buy these days, it also frees your team to focus on later-stage deals.
3. **Built-in discovery and qualification.** AI agents don’t just answer questions, they ask them, too. Company size, use cases, current tech stack, priorities, plus what features prospects choose to explore – all that data flows back to your sales team, helping reps and SEs (1) figure out which accounts are worth pursuing and (2) customize live demos accordingly.


Where Agentic Demos Fit in the Sales Cycle


Agentic demos fit best in the early stages of the sales cycle – before a prospect is ready to spend time talking to an SE or AE.


[Elizabeth Johnstone](http://linkedin.com/in/elizabeth-jp?originalSubdomain=ca) , Customer Education and Enablement Manager at[Productboard](https://www.productboard.com/) , calls agents “scalable backups” to live demos.


*“They give low-touch and self-serve prospects a real, interactive product experience 24/7, especially when they're interested but not quite ready to hop on a call with a human,”* she notes.


For these reasons, agentic demos tend to work particularly well for two types of buyers:


### Buyers Who Don’t Know What They Want Yet


These prospects sense they need to make a change. But they’re not sure what that change looks like or whether your product is the right fit.


*“At this point, the barrier to entry of speaking to a rep is a bit too high. They need some education to convert into a hotter lead, and that’s what an agentic demo can provide,”* Alex explains.


At the same time, they hook qualified prospects early and drop them straight into the sales cycle.


[Matt Finch](https://www.linkedin.com/in/mattfinch1/) , founder of Demo Atelier, points out: *“Buyers are so enabled by AI these days that it’s probably **costing** you deals to make them go through two, three, four disco calls.”*


### Buyers Who Don’t Have Much Time


A prospect might be interested in your product, but they’re probably examining five or six other vendors. They want to make as informed a decision as they can in as little time as possible.


*“They want you to show them what you’ve got without putting them through an hour or two hours worth of discovery calls,”* Alex emphasizes.


You could also send agentic demos to specific decision makers who are strapped for time.


*“A CFO, for example, is not going to jump on a call,”* says Alex. *“Oftentimes, giving them a five-minute thing to look at and get a feel for what they’re buying can be enough to get their seal of approval.”*


A shorter warm-up doesn’t just benefit the buyer.


Agents provide a transcript of the conversation, showing reps and SEs what use cases a prospect asked about, where they might’ve pushed back or gotten confused, so they’re not starting from zero with discovery.


[Muskan Jindal](https://www.navattic.com/blog/the-sales-engineer-playbook-for-ai-powered-discovery) , founding sales engineer at[Malachyte](https://www.malachyte.com/) , says, *“I see agents as a way to enable better discovery, or at least enable the customer to be more open to a broader discovery.”*


Why Most Teams Should Start with SMB


The[use cases for agentic demos](https://www.navattic.com/blog/where-to-use-ai-demo-agents) are broad, but adopting them requires a leap of faith. After all, you’re handing part of your sales process to a technology that is still maturing.


That’s why Alex recommends introducing agentic demos to SMB customers.


*“I think the safest cohort to test agentic demos on is SMB because they’re high volume, they’re typically the lowest ARR/ACV, and the buyer expectations might be a bit more agile than that of a legacy-type customer.”*


SMB buyers tend to identify problems quickly and want to solve them fast, which makes them a natural fit for agentic demos.


They may also have a higher tolerance for mistakes than an enterprise buyer, who may expect more of a white-glove experience from start to finish.


There’s also a practical capacity argument. SMB pipelines can be tens of thousands of leads long.


Sales won’t ever be able to reach those customers without help. And putting SEs on those calls wouldn’t make sense, given the likely low ACV.


*“Agentic demos can greatly augment and greatly extend the capacity of your workforce,”* Alex shares.


*“You can serve leads you may not have had the human hours to reach otherwise with the same level of care as an SE or sales rep.”*


Nectar, an employee experience platform, is already saving SE and AE time by deploying the Navattic agent for demo requests from prospects outside their ICP.


According to[Peyton Walbeck](https://www.linkedin.com/in/peyton-walbeck/) , Nectar’s VP of Marketing, *“It gives these prospects a simple, self-guided way to evaluate our product and determine fit, while freeing up our sales team's calendars to focus their time on strike zone opportunities.”*


### Where You Would Not Use an Agentic Demo


Alex was candid about the limitations of agentic demos. *“Late-stage deals will still require a human demo. At least for the next year or two before the tech really gets firing.”*


The key, he says, is to meet the buyer where they are.


*“If a buyer is happy to buy without a human demo, fantastic. If they want to buy with a human demo, fantastic. Whatever way a buyer wants to buy, you should be able to accommodate them.”*


Best Practices for Adopting Agentic Demos


Today’s buyers are skeptical. As MJ highlights, *“When it’s so easy to craft a picture-perfect demo, people start to question how a product truly behaves.”*


[AI agents](https://www.navattic.com/blog/top-ai-agentic-sales-tools) can help change those people’s minds by showing, in real time, exactly how your product works and answering any questions they might have.


Assuming, of course, the agent works.


One of the biggest concerns teams have about agentic demos is hallucination. To minimize that as much as possible:


### Build a Structured Knowledge Base


Before he does any work on an agent, Alex works with his clients to build a very large knowledge base.


*“We extract the features, the business value, and the use cases from recorded demos that we’d delivered to real customers,”* Alex shares. *“All of that goes into a massive data table, which we then feed to the agent.”*


From there, they map click paths to specific pieces of knowledge. When a buyer clicks a button, the agent knows exactly what it's allowed to say about that feature, nothing more.


*“If it doesn't know the answer, we tell it to say, ‘I don't know,’ and then hand the prospect off to an AE or log the question for follow-up.”*


### Get the Right People Involved Early


A lot of departments will want to have a say in what[agentic demos](https://www.navattic.com/blog/best-ai-demo-software) look like, but sales engineer input should carry the most weight.


*“I personally think that sales engineering is best placed to own agentic demos, with consultation from other departments,”* Alex says.


*“SEs know the product intimately, and can work with product marketing on positioning based on sales stage, and with marketing on where in the cycle the demo should be deployed.”*


Ownership also comes up when deciding whether to build an agent in-house or buy one.


With AI, it’s tempting to spin up your own.


But as Matt points out, the cost of a homegrown tool goes beyond development and hosting.


“What happens if the person who built it leaves the company? What else could you be building with that time? That money?”


### Test Aggressively


Remember, buyers can ask agents anything they want, which means you’ll need to control what agents say. Stress test for every kind of angle you can think of. For example:


- Would the agent give up sensitive information? (about customers? About the company? About the product roadmap?)
- Would it trash a competitor?
- Would it reveal pricing when it shouldn’t?


*“Sales engineers should be a part of that testing, helping tear it apart from every angle. I wouldn’t put an agentic demo in front of customers unless SEs say it’s good to go,”* Alex advises.


**Note:** you don’t have to go big bang with your rollout.


In fact, Matt suggests a “crawl-walk-run approach.” Do the same with agentic demos: start small, review transcripts, and iterate.


Measuring the Performance of Agentic & Interactive Demos


Tracking the success of agentic demos isn’t too different from how you’d measure[demo automation](https://www.navattic.com/blog/6-best-demo-automation-tools) or any other GTM motion. Pay attention to:


- **Pipeline creation and integrity. **** *“If you create half a million dollars in pipeline in a human way, you want to be able to create the same amount in an agentic way,”* says Alex.
- **Deal velocity.** How long does it take between a prospect requesting a demo and actually seeing one? Typically[takes two calls](https://www.navattic.com/report/state-of-demo-automation-2026) before a prospect ever reaches an SE. Ideally agentic demos compress that time.
- **Deal size.** Though keep in mind if you only train the agent on a subset of your product, buyers won’t be exposed to the full suite, and deal value could shrink.
- **Cost of acquisition.** How much does it cost to close a deal with an agentic demo in the mix versus without?


*“Those are some of the key metrics I recommend tracking, but it’ll be different for every company,”* Alex points out. *“For example, if your marketing team is more involved, they might care more about lead conversion. It depends on the KPIs your execs care about.”*

The Future of Agentic Demos in Sales


Agentic demos won’t replace human sellers –[now, or ever](https://www.navattic.com/blog/the-future-of-the-se-role) .


As Matt says, *“There will always be a place for the in-person demo that’s highly customized, ultra specific to the discovery you’ve done.”*


Alex tends to agree. *“Ultimately, people buy from people, and I think they always will.”*


But those premier demos should be reserved for the end of the sales cycle.


Before that, agents can:


- **Protect your team’s time.** *“Looking out 1-2 years, we see agents handling the first-touch Q&A and personalized product walkthroughs so our sales and SE teams can spend their time on the conversations that really need a human,”* says Elizabeth.
- **Serve whole buying committees.** *“Agents allow every decision maker to see the exact product features that matter to them,”* says Peyton.
- **Standardize the TOFU experience.** Per Peyton, “ *Agents make sure our pitch stays clear and accurate even when our sales rep isn’t in the room.”*
- **Give reps and SEs insights they can use.** Knowing what a prospect really wants is a solid foundation for building a lasting relationship. *“As things get more automated in this AI world, the human relationship actually becomes more important than it’s ever been,”* says Alex.
